dailyBrief.text: Good morning, Smileys — it's homecoming day: Benji is expected to be discharged today, with his first pediatrician appointment already booked for tomorrow, and Solon is giving you a beautiful day for it, mostly sunny with a high near 73°. It is also Election Day: Ohio polls are open 6:30 AM to 7:30 PM, the governor's race between Amy Acton and Vivek Ramaswamy and the Senate race between Jon Husted and Sherrod Brown are both close, and 66 Cuyahoga County precincts — including some in Solon — have new polling places, so check yours before you go. Overnight the U.S. carried out limited strikes on Iranian missile targets on Qeshm Island while talks remained possible, and the Cavs lost a close one to Oklahoma City, 117-112, despite the game staying tight into the final minute. Tonight, after the ride home and a first evening as a family of four (plus Moose), the results start rolling in after Ohio polls close at 7:30.

U.S. strikes Iran's Qeshm Island, Tehran says a peace deal is still far away and oil jumps
items.summary:
Oil climbed on Tuesday after the United States struck targets on Iran's Qeshm Island and a senior Iranian official said the two sides remained far from a deal to end the war. Brent crude rose $1.84 to $106.61 a barrel, while U.S. crude added $1.60 to $98.06.

An American official described the strike as defensive, aimed at surface-to-air missiles and at stopping Iran from threatening commercial shipping near the Strait of Hormuz. Iranian state media reported explosions on Qeshm, which hosts a naval base and an underground missile site near the mouth of the strait, and Iran's Revolutionary Guard claimed, without independent verification, that it had shot down two U.S. drones south of the island.

The war, which began in late February, has pushed up gasoline prices for months and was a central pressure on voters heading into Tuesday's midterms. An interim agreement in June was meant to wind hostilities down, but Tehran says it will not accept what it calls excessive American demands.

Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Qalibaf, Tehran's chief negotiator, said Iran had given Washington a strong and rational response and that the ball was now in the U.S. court. Watch shipping through Hormuz and whether mediated talks restart before either side strikes again.

items.title: Russia, Ukraine and the U.S. will hold their first direct talks since February in Abu Dhabi on Nov. 10-11
items.summary:
The Kremlin confirmed on Tuesday that Russia will sit down with Ukraine and the United States in Abu Dhabi on November 10 and 11, in the first direct Ukraine-Russia talks since February. U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff announced the round on Monday; he and Jared Kushner will lead the American side, while Vladimir Medinsky, an aide to President Vladimir Putin, will lead Moscow's delegation.

The agenda, as described by Witkoff and President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, covers ending the war, post-war security guarantees, de-escalation and humanitarian steps. Kyiv wants an energy ceasefire, a Black Sea truce to protect food exports, prisoner exchanges and the return of Ukrainian children. An earlier Abu Dhabi round in February produced an agreement to exchange 314 prisoners.

Putin agreed to the new round after meeting Witkoff in St. Petersburg two weeks ago, and American negotiators are meeting France, Germany, Britain, the EU and NATO in Brussels this week to discuss security guarantees.

Hosting Zelenskyy in Berlin on Tuesday, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Russia must show it is serious about a ceasefire, and that any lasting settlement has to involve Europeans, who have largely been shut out so far. The test next week is whether Abu Dhabi produces ceasefire language, not just another round of talks about talks.

items.title: Russia launches its biggest energy strike of the year: 289 drones and 76 missiles, three power plants offline
items.summary:
Russia pounded Ukraine's energy system in waves on Tuesday, launching 289 drones alongside 17 ballistic and 59 cruise missiles at power plants and substations from Odesa in the south to Rivne in the west. The barrage hit nine or ten regions, a week before peace talks are due to resume in Abu Dhabi.

DTEK, Ukraine's largest private power company, said three of its five thermal plants were knocked offline in what it called one of the most serious attacks it has faced. Emergency outages spread across Kyiv and at least six other regions, water supplies in the capital were disrupted, and Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal said three drones were aimed at a substation critical to the Khmelnytskyi nuclear plant, prompting Ukraine to notify the international atomic watchdog. On Wednesday the Energy Ministry said the strikes had forced nuclear plants to reduce output, though no reactor was reported hit.

Ukraine struck back overnight, setting fire to a major oil refinery in Yaroslavl, Russia, according to Reuters. Russia's Defence Ministry said its targets were facilities supplying Ukraine's military.

The timing matters for two reasons: winter is coming, and both sides are trying to improve their leverage before November 10. A grid that enters those talks still dark is a very different negotiating position than one that has been repaired.

items.title: Iranian leaders gloat over Trump's midterm defeat, but Tehran stays on high alert for new U.S. strikes
items.summary:
Iran's government openly savoured the Democrats' capture of both the House and Senate on Wednesday, declaring that American voters had rejected President Trump's war — even as Tehran remained on high alert for renewed American strikes.

Parliament Speaker Qalibaf posted about the result on X, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei issued a written statement blaming enduring U.S. hostility, and the newspaper Hamshahri put a blindfolded, bowed Trump on its front page under a headline about Iran's shadow over the elections. The coverage deliberately linked the vote to the 47th anniversary of the 1979 seizure of the U.S. embassy in Tehran.

Two senior Iranian sources told Reuters that Tehran welcomed the Democratic victory but feared Trump might answer a political defeat with a military strike. Iranian officials had earlier told Reuters they deliberately drew out negotiations to weaken Trump politically before the vote, and Trump himself acknowledged in two interviews that the war played a role in the Republican losses, while declining on Tuesday to rule out resuming combat.

Mediators are now intensifying efforts to end a war that has spread to Lebanon and Yemen, severely disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and hit Iran's economy through an American naval blockade. The risk runs both ways: Tehran is planning a wider response if the fighting resumes.

items.title: Rich countries fall far short on climate help: $305 billion a year needed, only $28.2 billion delivered
items.summary:
A new United Nations report released Wednesday puts hard numbers on the climate adaptation gap. Developing countries need about $305 billion a year to protect themselves from heat, floods, drought and rising seas, but developed countries delivered just $28.2 billion in 2024 — up only about $1 billion from the year before.

The UN Environment Programme's 2026 Adaptation Gap Report says the need will climb to roughly $420 billion a year by 2035. Even tripling adaptation finance, as agreed in the Brazil COP30 deal to $120 billion a year by 2035, would cover only about a fifth to a quarter of what is required. Temperatures are projected to pass the 1.5-degree threshold within a few years.

UNEP Executive Director Inger Andersen said the world is not ready, pointing to restoring ecosystems and strengthening infrastructure against heatwaves, droughts, wildfires and floods as the work that is not getting funded.

The numbers land days before COP31 talks open in Turkey on November 9 and run through November 20. Delegates there will also have to explain why nations are off track on the $300 billion a year in broader climate finance promised at COP29 in Baku.

items.title: Trump's midterm rebuke gives trading partners room to push back on his tariffs
items.summary:
The backlash over living costs, tariffs and the Iran war that handed Democrats both chambers of Congress could also embolden other countries to resist President Trump's trade demands, Reuters reported Wednesday.

China's fragile trade truce with Washington expires in January, and analysts say Beijing is likely to use Trump's weakened position as leverage. Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning called the midterms an internal U.S. matter on Wednesday while saying Beijing would manage differences and expand cooperation. India, meanwhile, says the first phase of its U.S. trade deal is in final drafting, but New Delhi will proceed only if it gains an advantage; an earlier framework cut a punitive tariff from 50% to 18%.

Japan and South Korea are also re-reading the deals they made last year, when they promised $550 billion and $350 billion respectively in U.S. investments. Executives told Reuters separately that a Democratic Congress is unlikely to ease firms' tariff costs quickly, because the administration has pursued tariffs through executive authority that does not need Congress.

Trump's next major outing is Asia later this month, meeting Southeast Asian leaders in the Philippines and then APEC in Shenzhen, China. Expect negotiating partners to play for time and see what the new Congress changes.

items.title: Democrats seize both the House and Senate in a sweeping midterm rebuke of Trump
items.summary:
Democrats took control of both chambers of Congress on Tuesday, winning in Republican strongholds for the first time in generations and ending unified Republican government for the final two years of President Trump's term. Republicans went in holding the Senate 53-47 and the House by a handful of seats; Democrats needed a net gain of four Senate seats and flipped at least seven — in Texas, North Carolina, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio, South Carolina and Maine.

The voter surveys explain the scale. About half of voters said their vote was a rebuke of the president, roughly three-quarters were angry or dissatisfied with the country's direction, and about seven in ten wanted stronger checks and balances. Democrats campaigned on affordability and corruption, blaming tariffs and the Iran war for higher costs, and early tallies showed Republicans losing ground in all but a handful of the roughly 1,700 counties counted on election night, with sharp Democratic gains in Latino counties.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer called it a generational remake of the Senate map. Trump accepted the outcome, congratulated Democrats, said he would work with them on immigration and threatened to veto bills he called insane, while also posting that he was not on the ballot.

The new Congress convenes January 3 and can investigate the administration, demand concessions and block nominees, including to the Supreme Court. Democrats do not have the two-thirds majorities needed to override vetoes, and a few Senate races, including Alaska and Mississippi, were still uncalled early Wednesday.

items.title: James Talarico flips Texas Senate seat — first Democrat to win statewide there since 1994
items.summary:
Texas state Rep. James Talarico, a 37-year-old former teacher and seminarian, defeated Trump-backed Attorney General Ken Paxton to win a U.S. Senate seat, ending a 32-year Democratic losing streak in Texas statewide races. It is the party's first Texas Senate win since Lloyd Bentsen's re-election in 1988, for a seat no Democrat has held since 1961.

With nearly 98% of precincts reporting, the Associated Press count had Talarico at about 5.44 million votes to Paxton's 4.25 million — in a state Trump carried by 14 points in 2024. The race was the most expensive Senate contest in U.S. history, with advertising tallies above $570 million; Republicans spent more than $316 million trying to hold the seat, and Elon Musk put $168 million into super PACs backing Paxton.

Paxton carried heavy baggage — a 2023 impeachment, a securities fraud case and a divorce — and he had ousted Senator John Cornyn in the May Republican primary after Trump's endorsement, a choice many Republican leaders privately viewed as the weaker general-election path. Talarico, who beat Rep. Jasmine Crockett in the Democratic primary, was the race's top fundraiser and made big gains with Latino voters.

The result puts Texas, with its 40 electoral votes, credibly in play for 2028. Talarico will be sworn in on January 3, 2027.

items.title: Democrats win a majority of governorships, with historic firsts in Texas, Georgia and Florida
items.summary:
Thirty-six states chose governors on Tuesday, and Democrats emerged with a majority of governorships for the first time in two decades — at least 27 of the nation's governor's offices in 2027, flipping Texas, Georgia, Ohio, Iowa and, in some tallies, Nevada while holding 17 others.

In Texas, Gina Hinojosa beat three-term Governor Greg Abbott to become the state's first Latina governor and its first Democratic governor in more than 30 years, despite Abbott's war chest of more than $100 million. In Georgia, former Atlanta mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms defeated billionaire Rick Jackson to become the first Black woman elected governor of any U.S. state. Ohio elected Amy Acton, California chose Xavier Becerra as its first Latino governor, and New Mexico elected Deb Haaland, the first Native American woman to govern a state.

Republicans did make history of their own in Florida, where Rep. Byron Donalds, backed by Trump, narrowly beat David Jolly to succeed the term-limited Ron DeSantis, becoming Florida's first Black governor.

A Democratic majority of governors strengthens the party's hand against the Trump agenda at state level — and gives it control of election administration and redistricting machinery in more states heading into 2028, plus a fresh bench of national figures.

items.title: Vance says 'the reason we lost is the war' — Trump says Iran was only 'a piece of it'
items.summary:
The Republican argument over why Tuesday was so bad started in public on Wednesday. Vice President JD Vance, in a long post on X, put the blame squarely on the Iran war: the reason the party lost, he wrote, is the war, adding that the president himself said so on election night.

Vance argued turnout was not the problem — voters who backed Trump in 2024 showed up, but many voted Democratic this time. Citing a pollster, he listed the switchers' reasons: end the war, bring down the cost of living, an America First agenda, and rejection of the current U.S.-Israel relationship.

Trump gave a different account. He told The Wall Street Journal on election night that Iran was a piece of it, said he had done the right thing and would do it again, and suggested oil prices, rather than the war itself, were the liability. After roughly three hours of silence he posted on Truth Social that he was not on the ballot and would have won in a landslide, and he also blamed candidates and Fox News coverage.

That public split matters beyond blame: it signals a fight over the party's direction and the 2028 succession, and it increases pressure from inside the administration's own camp to bring the Iran war to an end.

items.title: Jeffries poised to become the first Black Speaker, Schumer returns as Majority Leader
items.summary:
When the new Congress convenes on January 3, 2027, both chambers are set to be led by New Yorkers. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, 56, is on path to become the first Black Speaker of the House, succeeding Mike Johnson, and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer told reporters Wednesday he was confident he would be re-elected as leader — this time as Majority Leader.

Jeffries still needs a caucus nomination and a floor vote, but no serious challenger has been reported. Before the election he promised Democrats would aggressively prepare to move fast from January 3, and the party's clearest tools are oversight and investigations, control of spending bills, and the Senate's power to block Trump's nominees.

Jeffries also claimed a redistricting victory, saying Democrats had crushed the Republican gerrymander across the country — a reference to the state-by-state map fight that was supposed to protect the Republican House majority and largely did not.

There are limits: with no veto-proof majorities, legislation still needs Trump's signature. And the first test of divided government comes early — federal funding runs out on December 11, before the new Congress is even seated.

items.title: Stocks surge as Democrats sweep the midterms — Dow jumps about 1,300 points
items.summary:
Wall Street roared on Wednesday as investors digested the Democratic sweep. The Dow Jones Industrial Average surged about 1,307 points, or 2.5%, on pace for its best day since April, while the S&P 500 rose 1.5% and the Nasdaq Composite gained 1.7%. The VIX fear index sank 16%.

The day began very differently. Overnight, Nasdaq-100 futures fell as much as 2.4% and S&P futures dropped 1.4%, before reversing after President Trump accepted the results and said he was willing to work with the opposition. Investors warmed to divided government as a brake on extreme policy in either direction; Deutsche Bank's George Saravelos said a large Democratic majority plus Trump's willingness to deal should reduce risk premiums. Bond yields steadied after an early dip and the dollar weakened.

Beneath the rally, the AI trade split. Nvidia slipped about 1%, an AI infrastructure fund fell more than 7%, and Tesla and SpaceX shares dropped amid fears that Democratic wins in states like Texas would bring data-centre moratoriums. Amazon rose more than 6% in early trading, and Meta and Alphabet also gained.

Next up for markets: final election counts, the Democrats' policy priorities, Qualcomm and Arm earnings after Wednesday's close, and Friday's October jobs report.

items.title: AMD's data-centre sales nearly double, and it guides fourth-quarter revenue to about $17 billion
items.summary:
AMD reported third-quarter results after Tuesday's close that beat expectations on the strength of its AI business. Revenue rose 45% to $13.38 billion, ahead of the $13.09 billion analysts expected, and adjusted earnings of $2.09 a share also topped forecasts. The stock rose in after-hours trading.

Data-centre revenue jumped 97% to a record $8.55 billion, and now accounts for 64% of AMD's sales, up from 47% a year ago. The growth came from fifth-generation EPYC server processors and the first revenue shipments of its MI455 accelerators and Helios rack systems, as AI spending shifts toward running models, not just training them.

The rest of the business shows how concentrated the boom is: gaming revenue fell 40% to $773 million, while client chips grew a modest 7% to $2.95 billion. An inventory build also cut into free cash flow.

AMD guided fourth-quarter revenue to about $17 billion, above the $16.23 billion consensus, with adjusted gross margin around 55%. It remains Nvidia's main challenger in AI chips, and it expects AI chip revenue to overtake server CPU revenue in the fourth quarter.

items.title: Super Micro's revenue nearly quadruples to $20 billion on AI server demand
items.summary:
Super Micro Computer reported fiscal first-quarter sales of $19.95 billion on Tuesday, nearly four times the $5.02 billion of a year earlier and well above analyst estimates in the $16.4 billion to $17.5 billion range. Shares jumped more than 9% after hours, and net income came in at $1.59 billion.

AI solutions made up 71% of revenue, up from 59% the prior quarter, and large data-centre and appliance revenue grew 321% year over year to $14.7 billion. Chief Executive Charles Liang credited a rapid shift toward selling complete AI and IT data-centre solutions rather than individual servers.

There are risks inside the boom: a single large customer accounted for 44% of revenue, operations used $434 million in cash as inventory and receivables grew, and guided gross margins of roughly 12% to 12.5% are thin for the scale involved.

Super Micro raised its full-year forecast to $72 billion to $82 billion, from $65 billion to $72 billion, and guided the December quarter to $19.5 billion to $21.5 billion. Whatever voters think of data centres, hyperscaler spending is still flowing to the companies that build the servers.

items.title: The election stiffens the Federal Reserve's guardrails, but its independence risks remain
items.summary:
The Democratic sweep, and Senate control in particular, strengthens the Federal Reserve's defences against President Trump's efforts to influence it, Reuters reported Wednesday — because the Senate confirms the Fed's seven-member board, and a Democratic Senate can block Trump from seating more allies.

It also creates new headaches for Chair Kevin Warsh. Oversight committees flip to the Democrats, and Senator Elizabeth Warren, a sharp Warsh critic, is likely to replace Tim Scott as chair of the Senate Banking Committee, with power to investigate matters such as Warsh's handling of hundreds of millions of dollars in assets. The House Financial Services Committee flips as well. Three current board members are Biden appointees, and former Chair Jerome Powell remains on the board — a configuration Trump has called hostile while demanding drastic rate cuts as policymakers have been raising rates to fight inflation.

The sharpest fight is over Governor Lisa Cook. Trump's effort to fire her is expected to move through a White House administrative process in the coming weeks, with a court challenge likely; the Supreme Court has already ruled against Trump once in the Cook matter.

Watch the December Fed decision, the Cook proceeding, and Warren's committee agenda when the new Congress convenes in January. Democratic committees could also complicate bank and crypto regulatory reforms the administration wants.

items.title: U.S. services growth cools slightly in October, but prices stay stubbornly high
items.summary:
America's services sector grew a little more slowly in October while still expanding, according to the Institute for Supply Management survey released Wednesday. The nonmanufacturing index dipped to 54.5 from 54.9 in September, just under the 54.8 forecast — a reading above 50 means growth, and it suggests the economy began the fourth quarter on solid footing.

Underneath the headline, new orders moderated and supply chains stayed strained. The prices-paid index eased only slightly, to a still-high 73.0 from 74.0, while services employment improved to 51.4 from 50.1.

That price pressure is the problem for the Federal Reserve. Economists expect inflation to stay above the Fed's 2% target into 2027. The Fed held its benchmark rate at 3.75% to 4.00% last week while acknowledging inflation remains elevated, and economists expect it to raise borrowing costs in December.

Friday's government jobs report is the next big data point: economists surveyed by Reuters expect payrolls to have risen 65,000 in October, after 29,000 in September, with unemployment steady at 4.2%.

items.title: Private payrolls rose 86,000 in October, beating forecasts, ADP says
items.summary:
Private employers added 86,000 jobs in October, the ADP National Employment Report said Wednesday, matching September's downwardly revised 86,000 and beating the 69,000 gain economists polled by Reuters had expected. September was originally reported at 90,000.

The ADP report, produced with the Stanford Digital Economy Lab, arrives two days before the government's official employment numbers and is closely watched even though it has historically been a poor predictor of the official private payroll count.

Economists expect Friday's Bureau of Labor Statistics report to show private payrolls up about 64,000 in October, after 46,000 in September, with total payrolls up 65,000 and unemployment unchanged at 4.2%.

That picture — hiring that is modest but not collapsing, alongside inflation that remains too high — is exactly what makes the Federal Reserve's December decision difficult. A much stronger or weaker Friday print would move that debate, and markets with it.

items.title: Trump says he will wield the 'power of veto' — but is prepared to work with Democrats
items.summary:
After Democrats seized both chambers of Congress, President Trump told Fox News by phone that he was prepared to work with them, while stressing the one power divided government cannot take away. He has the power of veto, he said, and that power is impervious, adding that he has a lot of Democratic friends who want to talk.

Trump conceded that the war in Iran played a role in the Republican losses, while saying voters understood its importance, and he credited the opposition: Democrats, he said, did a good job and fought hard. The messaging was mixed, though — he also posted a photo of a red VETO hat on Truth Social, the White House posted that Trump is still your president, and on election night he had distanced himself by noting he was not on the ballot.

The arithmetic is the story. Overriding a veto takes two-thirds of both chambers, which Democrats do not have, so Trump's signature remains necessary for any law. At the same time he is now a lame duck in his final two years, and a Democratic Senate can block any Supreme Court nomination.

Trump had no public events scheduled Wednesday. Watch for personnel changes and the first signals on a budget deal before the new Congress convenes in January; Trump told The Wall Street Journal he could find common ground on the budget, foreign policy and housing.

items.title: How Trump and Republicans lost the midterms, according to the AP Voter Poll
items.summary:
The AP Voter Poll, a survey of voters in all 50 states conducted for the Associated Press and major networks, finds an electorate exhausted with President Trump after a decade at the centre of American politics — and it shows in the result: Democrats won back both the House and the Senate.

Inflation did the deepest damage. Trump had promised to tame prices, and by voters' judgment he failed to deliver, with conditions worsening instead. About two-thirds of voters said Trump's policies had made the economy worse, and roughly eight in ten of those voters backed Democrats. In Texas, about two in ten voters said inflation had caused them severe hardship, and about three-quarters of them voted for Democrat James Talarico for Senate. Voters also blamed tariffs and the Iran war, more than half called government corruption crucial to their vote, and about seven in ten — including roughly four in ten Republicans — said Congress is not providing enough checks and balances.

There is a warning for the winners inside the same data: only about half of voters view the Democratic Party favourably, and its edge on the economy is slim. Many swing voters chose Democrats without liking them much.

That sets a high bar for the incoming Democratic Congress: it was elected largely on cost of living, and it will be judged on whether daily costs actually come down.

items.title: Voters overwhelmingly reject AI data centres on midterm ballots — and Ohio led the revolt
items.summary:
Data centres were on the ballot in about 41 to 45 local measures across 10 states on Tuesday, and the builders lost almost everywhere. By early Wednesday, 33 measures restricting the facilities had passed, with several more projected for the anti-data-centre side.

Ohio delivered the strongest rebuke. The state, which is home to about 257 data centres, already had 125 local moratoriums and has some $40 billion in planned investment through 2030, put 20 or 21 measures before voters — and restrictions won or were projected to win in every one. Urbana and Hubbard approved outright bans with about 77% support, Trenton voted 80-20 to ban an 18-building Amazon campus, Granville backed a ban at 82%, and Piqua recalled commissioners while passing a ban where Meta plans a centre.

The politics are now bigger than zoning. Polling cited in coverage found 55% of Ohio adults oppose new construction and 65% oppose tax breaks, and a network exit poll found more than half of voters called AI and data centres a crucial or major factor. Texas, Georgia and Ohio also elected Democratic governors who campaigned on pauses or crackdowns.

All of these results are unofficial until certification, which in Ohio is due by November 24. The stakes are national, though: a $10 trillion AI buildout now has to run through thousands of local governments that just voted no.

items.title: Floodwaters leave a sea of mud and shattered homes in the Southwest; Florida is soaked too
items.summary:
Skies cleared on Tuesday, but after almost two weeks of on-and-off heavy rain, parts of the Southwest were still underwater Wednesday while others began digging out of the mud. By one estimate from former NOAA chief scientist Ryan Maue, more than 20 trillion gallons of rain — about ten months of Niagara Falls' flow — fell on the Four Corners states and Nevada in two weeks.

Fifteen river gauges in Arizona, Colorado and New Mexico set all-time record crests on November 1. In Arizona, the Verde River flooded at record levels, leaving an RV park in Camp Verde strewn with mobile homes and vehicles, and Governor Katie Hobbs declared a state of emergency on Monday. Pagosa Springs, Colorado, saw a home swept off its foundation, a closed downtown and collapsed bridges, while homes in Durango were buried in about two feet of mud. A 73-year-old man died in floodwaters in Flagstaff, and evacuation orders affecting at least 20,000 people in San Juan County, New Mexico, were expected to lift soon as rivers crested lower than feared.

Florida was hit separately: Brevard County has had more than two feet of rain since Sunday, Palm Beach County more than 20 inches, at least 20 polling places were moved on Election Day, and Palm Beach County closed ten schools Wednesday for localised flooding. Melbourne recorded 11.51 inches on November 2, its wettest day in 89 years.

Forecasters warned of more flash flooding on Florida's southeast coast Wednesday, a marginal excessive-rain risk in the Ohio and Tennessee valleys, and snow in the central Rockies.

items.title: A Washington resident is the first U.S. bird flu death of 2026
items.summary:
A Yakima County, Washington resident who had been exposed to infected dairy cows has died of bird flu, officials announced Sunday — the first known U.S. bird flu death of 2026 and the third since the H5N1 virus jumped into dairy cattle in February 2024. The patient, who had underlying conditions, was hospitalised on October 31 with a severe case and died November 1; close contacts are being monitored.

Yakima County has now had three human cases this year, all since mid-October and all linked to infected cows: a mild case in a dairy worker on October 15 that was the first human case in nearly a year, the fatal case, and a third mild case reported over the weekend. Washington confirmed its first cattle infections on October 8 at two Yakima farms, and the count has grown to roughly 33 to 40 herds, nearly all in Yakima County. On November 2 the USDA announced the first detection of the same B3.13 genotype in Indiana, in two connected Newton County dairy herds.

Nationwide there have been more than 72 human cases since 2024 and about 1,222 infected herds in 21 states. No human-to-human transmission has ever been documented in the United States, and officials say the risk to the public remains low.

Experts warn the concern is timing: a fall bird flu uptick arriving with the start of seasonal flu season raises the risk of the viruses mixing. The Yakima Health District updates its human case count on Mondays and Thursdays, and the CDC dashboard had not yet added Washington's three cases.

items.title: Amy Acton wins Ohio governor's race, the first woman elected to the job
items.summary:
Democrat Dr. Amy Acton, who led Ohio's health department through the early COVID pandemic, defeated Trump-backed Republican Vivek Ramaswamy to become Ohio's next governor. She is the first woman elected governor in state history — Republican Nancy Hollister previously held the office for 11 days in 1999 without being elected — and the first Democrat to win the governorship since Ted Strickland in 2006.

The unofficial numbers were not close. The Ohio Secretary of State's tally, cited by the Columbus Dispatch, had Acton at 52.3% to Ramaswamy's 44.3%, with Libertarian Don Kissick at about 3.4%; the Associated Press, at 98% of precincts reporting, counted 2,404,178 votes for Acton to 2,039,730 for Ramaswamy. Neither candidate had previously held elected office, and Acton succeeds the term-limited Governor Mike DeWine, under whom she served as health director. Ramaswamy even lost Hamilton County, where about 63% backed Acton, though he carried Butler, Warren and Clermont counties.

The Dispatch's Wednesday analysis framed the night as Ohio Democrats' biggest in 20 years, built on campaigning about affordability.

Acton will be sworn in on January 11, 2027, at the Ohio Statehouse for a four-year term. All results remain unofficial until they are certified.

items.title: Sherrod Brown wins back a U.S. Senate seat, beating Jon Husted
items.summary:
Former Senator Sherrod Brown is going back to Washington. The 73-year-old Democrat ousted appointed Republican Senator Jon Husted in the special election for the Ohio seat JD Vance gave up to become vice president, in a race the AP, NBC and CNN all called for Brown.

It is a rare comeback: Brown lost re-election in 2024 to Bernie Moreno after 18 years in the Senate, and reports note he is the first former senator to regain a seat after losing re-election since Slade Gorton in 1988. Husted, the former lieutenant governor appointed by Governor DeWine in January 2025, will leave office December 15 under state law. Brown will serve the rest of Vance's term, through January 3, 2029, which means he must run again in 2028 to keep it.

Unofficial Secretary of State figures had Brown at 50.1% to Husted's 45.2%, and the AP count at 98% reporting was 2,301,042 votes to 2,077,748. It was one of the most expensive Senate races in history, with roughly $500 million in advertising.

Brown's win was one of seven Republican Senate seats Democrats flipped nationally, and a necessary brick in the party's new Senate majority.

items.title: Ohio voters overwhelmingly put photo voter ID into the state constitution
items.summary:
Ohio voters approved Issue 3 by roughly two to one on Tuesday, writing the state's photo ID requirement for voting into the Ohio Constitution. The Associated Press declared the amendment winning at 9:33 p.m. on election night, and at 98% of precincts reporting the count stood at 2,934,245 yes votes to 1,556,864 no votes.

The amendment enshrines the existing state law requiring government-issued photo ID to vote in person. Accepted identification in coverage of the measure includes an unexpired Ohio driver's licence or state ID, a U.S. passport or passport card, and military, Ohio National Guard or VA identification. Mail voting uses photo ID or a signature plus another specified identifier, with a possible legislative alternative for voters with a sincere religious objection to being photographed.

Supporters argued that putting the rule in the constitution locks it in against future lawmakers weakening it. Critics countered that it was unnecessary, because Ohio already has a photo ID law and there is little evidence of widespread fraud.

One clarification from Signal Ohio's voter guide: Issue 3 concerns voter ID only — it does not add a proof-of-citizenship requirement. Results remain unofficial until certified.

items.title: Ohio Democrats win 8 of 15 U.S. House seats in a night of upsets
items.summary:
Ohio Democrats won eight of the state's 15 U.S. House seats on Tuesday, flipping three Republican-held districts — an outcome the Columbus Dispatch called almost unimaginable after Republicans redrew the congressional map in their own favour.

The flips: in the Columbus-area 15th District, newcomer Don Leonard, a former Ohio State professor, beat Rep. Mike Carey about 52% to 45%. In the Dayton-area 10th, Kristina Knickerbocker beat Rep. Mike Turner, a former Dayton mayor who had served in Congress for 23 years, by roughly 49% to 47%. And in the 7th District in northeast Ohio, Brian Poindexter beat Max Miller with about 55%. Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur, the longest-serving woman in Congress, held the Toledo-area 9th District with about 52% despite repeated redraws aimed at her seat, and Rep. Joyce Beatty won Columbus's 3rd District 77% to 23%.

The sweep ran down the ballot too: per unofficial returns cited by the Dispatch, Democrats broke the Republican supermajority in the Ohio House, gained two Ohio Senate seats, and won attorney general, secretary of state and treasurer, plus two Ohio Supreme Court seats.

Analysts told the Dispatch to be careful about the lesson: they read the night as a referendum on President Trump, not proof that Ohio has turned blue. Certification will make the results official.

items.title: Brook Park ironworker Brian Poindexter ousts Rep. Max Miller in the Cleveland-area district
items.summary:
Democrat Brian Poindexter, a union ironworker and Brook Park city council member, unseated two-term Republican Rep. Max Miller in Ohio's 7th District, which covers southern and western Cuyahoga County plus Medina and Ashland counties and northern Wayne County. NBC News and Decision Desk HQ projected Poindexter the winner, and Miller conceded late Tuesday.

The scale of the flip is striking: the district backed Trump by 11 points in 2024, and Miller won re-election that year by almost 15. Unofficial Secretary of State returns had Poindexter at 54.9% to Miller's 45.1% — 180,614 votes to 148,177 — and Poindexter slightly outraised Miller, $3.7 million to $3.2 million in filings through mid-October.

The race was dominated by Miller's divorce and custody fight, including abuse allegations from his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, which Miller vehemently denied and sought to rebut with documents and audio. A Cuyahoga County children-services investigation into their toddler's broken collarbone found insufficient evidence of abuse or neglect. Poindexter campaigned on his union background and the cost of living, blaming inflation on tariffs and Trump administration policies.

Poindexter's win was one of three House flips that gave Ohio Democrats eight of the state's 15 seats. Results remain unofficial until certified.

items.title: Pitch-rigging trial begins for Guardians pitchers Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz
items.summary:
Opening statements were set to begin Wednesday in Brooklyn federal court in the pitch-fixing trial of Cleveland Guardians pitchers Emmanuel Clase and Luis Ortiz, after a lengthy two-day jury selection wrapped up Tuesday. The two are being tried together and have pleaded not guilty.

They face conspiracy, wire fraud, money laundering and bribery-related charges carrying up to 65 years in prison if convicted on all counts. Prosecutors allege the pitchers threw certain pitches at predetermined times to benefit gamblers, with more than $450,000 in wagers involved. Clase, a three-time All-Star who was one of baseball's top closers, is accused of rigging at least 18 pitches across 17 games from May 2023 to May 2025, and prosecutors say he recruited Ortiz, who is accused over two pitches in June 2025. The defence is expected to argue the pitchers were varying pitch placement strategically, not colluding with gamblers.

Both men were placed on paid leave in July 2025 and moved to unpaid leave in March. Clase's five-year, $20 million contract expired after the 2026 season, leaving a $2 million buyout for 2027 and free agency pending the trial's outcome.

The trial is expected to last about three weeks, and potential witnesses include teammates and Guardians general manager Mike Chernoff. It is the first of five recent federal sports-gambling manipulation cases to reach a trial.

baby.tip: Homecoming day tip: before you leave the hospital, do the car-seat check while help is still right there — base tight, straps snug at armpit level, and Benji's first ride home in a rear-facing seat in the back. Then tonight, keep it simple: one bag unpacked, feeding log started, and the diaper bag restocked for tomorrow's first pediatrician visit. If anything about feeding, breathing or temperature worries you at home, call the pediatrician or your OB team — that's exactly what they're there for.
baby.fact: Newborns sleep a lot but in short stretches — typically 16 to 17 hours a day, broken into naps of just a few hours at a time, because their tiny stomachs need frequent feeding. Benji's sleep will feel random this first week; short, frequent stretches around the clock are completely normal for a brand-new baby.
baby.fun: Today's tiny mission: the first family photo at home — Mike, Kelly, Benji and Moose in one frame (Moose at a calm, supervised distance for take one). It doesn't need to be perfect; the slightly chaotic version is the one you'll love most in a year.
